summary: EPP provides commands to delete domain and host objects, which are used to publish DNS information. This best current practice document gives operational guidance for deletions so they avoid DNS resolution disruption and keep data consistent.

eli5.summary: Before throwing away an old street sign, check nobody still uses it for directions. This gives rules for removing domain records without breaking things.

questions: what is a sacrificial name server
how to delete a domain with host objects in epp
why is renaming epp hosts risky
subtitle: How registrars can delete domains and name server hosts in EPP without breaking DNS or opening the door to hijackers.

tldr.problem: EPP says a domain SHOULD NOT be deleted while host objects under it exist, and a host SHOULD NOT be deleted while other objects use it. Registrars worked around this by renaming hosts to made-up external names, which has let attackers take over DNS resolution.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes the observed and possible deletion practices, lists the benefits and detriments of each, and then requires servers and clients to implement one of three safe practices while marking the rest as NOT RECOMMENDED.
tldr.outcome: Renaming to a client-maintained sacrificial name server, restorable explicit deletion, or renaming under the special-use domain sacrificial.invalid are the approved routes. Renaming to presumed non-existent external hosts MUST NOT be used.

today: RFC 9874 is a Best Current Practice published in September 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the guidance in RFC 5731 and RFC 5732.

sections.title: The Deletion Dilemma
sections.content:
The EPP domain mapping (RFC 5731) says a domain object SHOULD NOT be deleted while subordinate host objects are associated with it. The host mapping (RFC 5732) says a host object SHOULD NOT be deleted while it is associated with any other object, because that can cause DNS resolution failure for the domains that refer to it.

This creates a dilemma. Suppose a client wants to delete example.com, but its host ns1.example.com is also used by domains sponsored by a different client. The first client cannot update those other domains, and it is advised not to delete the host. Some registrars therefore rename the host to a different, external name so the domain can go. That practice is what this Best Current Practice document examines.

The RFC explains the rationale for the SHOULD NOT text, describes the risks of renaming, and analyzes the practices that have been or could be used.
sections.eli5: You want to tear down your clubhouse, but your friend's treehouse uses a rope tied to it. You cannot touch your friend's treehouse, so people have been doing risky tricks to get around that.

sections.title: Why Deletion Is Discouraged
sections.content:
The RFC gives three reasons for the original advice.

  • DNS: deleting a domain makes the name servers under it unresolvable, and deleting a host makes every domain delegated to it unresolvable. Leaving hosts behind after their parent domain is deleted invites hijacking, since someone can re-register the domain and control resolution. It also creates orphan glue.
  • Client-server consistency: if a server silently deletes subordinate hosts, client and server disagree about what is still registered. The RFC notes that experience suggests this poses little operational risk.
  • Relational consistency: implementations may keep domains and hosts in a relational database, where removing a domain without handling its hosts can cause integrity problems.
sections.eli5: If you pull one brick out of a wall, other bricks may fall, and a stranger might sneak in through the gap. The advice is to take things apart one careful step at a time.

sections.title: The Risk of Renaming Hosts
sections.content:
Renaming a host so that it lives under a different parent domain turns it into an external host, which lets the original domain be deleted. The RFC walks through an example: ClientX registers domain1.example and its host ns1.domain1.example, which ClientY also uses for domain2.example. ClientX cannot change ClientY's domain, so it renames the host to ns1.example.org. A renamed host like this is called a sacrificial host.

If example.org does not exist, anyone can register it and create ns1.example.org. That name server then receives queries for every domain delegated to it, and its operator can answer maliciously. Other outcomes depend on the new name: if it offers recursive service or none, queries end in SERVFAIL and resolvers may requery aggressively. The RFC also notes that renaming a host to an external host cannot be reversed by the EPP client.

The sacrificial name is not harmless filler. If an attacker can register it, they control DNS resolution for domains still pointing at it.
sections.eli5: If you hand your friends a fake address for a house that does not exist, a sneaky person can build a house there and greet everyone who comes by.

sections.title: Renaming to Sacrificial Hosts
sections.content:
The first family of practices keeps domains delegated in the zone by renaming hosts. Benefits include that affected domains stay delegated and their registrars may be able to work out what happened. The detriment is that zones fill with irrelevant records that registrars and registrants must clean up.

Observed practices:

  • External, presumed non-existent hosts: convenient, but attackers have registered these parent domains and taken control of resolution. Sponsoring clients are not told. This MUST NOT be used.
  • AS112.ARPA names: a misuse of AS112, which exists for reverse lookups on non-unique addresses. It can cause trouble for intrusion detection systems and firewalls and needs infrastructure maintained.
  • Non-authoritative hosts such as glue pointing at public recursive services: queries fail with SERVFAIL and resolvers may requery aggressively. This MUST NOT be used.
  • Client-maintained dedicated sacrificial name servers: clients MAY do this. The client keeps the parent domain registered, the name must resolve to addresses, and the client MUST operate an authoritative name server there. The server MAY provide any valid response.

Potential practices (not observed in use): a pseudo-TLD such as .alt (MUST NOT be used), a reserved special-use TLD, a special-use domain, and a community-wide sacrificial name server service.
sections.eli5: Instead of just deleting the old mailbox, you point everyone to a spare mailbox that you look after yourself. That way nobody else can set up a fake one.

sections.title: Deleting Hosts Directly
sections.content:
The second family lets servers delete objects even when relationships exist, instead of renaming.

  • Implicit deletion: the server lets the sponsoring client delete a host and automatically disassociates it from other clients' domains. Observed in use. A downside is that domains could be left with no name servers (and be removed from the zone) or with only one.
  • Informing affected clients: for example through the EPP Change Poll extension (RFC 8590). Observed in use; it needs extra development and may strain scalability.
  • Explicit deletion requests, extra deletion details in the response (msg, reason or msgQ elements, plus the poll command): potential practices not yet observed.
  • Explicit deletion with restore: a domain with associated subordinate hosts is deleted only if the associations can be brought back with the restore operation of RFC 3915. Hosts can be kept in pendingDelete status with their associations, which removes them from the DNS but gives a preview of the deletion. Not yet observed in use.

The restore approach lets clients delete what they need while the server can undo a malicious or accidental action during the redemption period, though a single delete command now has wider side effects and large association counts may call for asynchronous processing.
sections.eli5: The shop takes down the sign for you, tells the neighbors, and keeps the old sign in a back room for a while in case it was a mistake.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
EPP servers and clients MUST implement one of these practices:

  • Rename host objects to a sacrificial name server host object maintained by the client.
  • Delete host objects and associations with the restore option, based on explicit client requests, while giving requesting clients additional deletion details and informing affected clients.
  • Rename host objects to a sacrificial name server host that uses a special-use domain, avoiding the issues described in RFC 8244. Using sacrificial.invalid as the parent domain is RECOMMENDED, to avoid the overhead of creating a new TLD that offers no extra operational benefit.

All other practices in the analysis are NOT RECOMMENDED because of undesired side effects.
sections.eli5: You may pick one of three safe ways to retire an old address. Every other trick is a bad idea.

sections.title: Security Notes and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC has no IANA actions. Its security discussion repeats that host renaming can introduce a risk of DNS resolution hijack. Child domains that depend on hosts sponsored by another client may be protected by DNSSEC, and by using hosts associated with multiple domain objects, though DNSSEC and multiple hosts may interfere with controlled-interruption IP addresses that alert registrants. EPP clients can periodically scan sponsored domains for association with sacrificial name servers and alert users.

It also warns that, without DNSSEC at the victim, an attacker who controls one name server may use CDS/CDNSKEY records to take over the domain completely if automated DS maintenance does not check all name servers for consistency, and CSYNC could let an attacker change the NS records.
sections.eli5: Even with good rules, a trickster who controls one signpost might try to rewrite the whole map, so grown-ups should check all the signposts agree.
